analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks and commodities.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referrals; it was introduced with 2 cosponsors and died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Ethics in Government Act to bar members of Congress and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, futures, commodities, or similar instruments while the member is in office. They could keep broad mutual funds, index ETFs, and Treasury securities, or place holdings in a blind trust, and would have 180 days to divest. Profits from violations would be turned over to the Treasury, violations could draw civil fines from the House and Senate ethics committees, and the Government Accountability Office would audit compliance. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want lawmakers making decisions about companies, regulations, and wars without a personal stake in the outcome. The bill targets a conflict of interest unique to the people who write the laws: members and their spouses trading the same stocks their work can move. It also benefits firms and markets by removing the chance that a legislator trades on nonpublic information, though the effect there is modest.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding, purchasing, or selling individual securities, security futures, commodities, and synthetic equivalents (like options) during the member's term of service [S2] [S3].
Allows diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury securities, and holdings in a qualified blind trust, so members can keep broad-market investments without company-specific stakes [S3].

Requires any profit made in violation to be disgorged to the Treasury, bars deducting the losses of violating trades from income tax, and allows civil fines from the House and Senate ethics committees [S2] [S3].
Requires each member to certify compliance annually, published on a public website, and directs the Government Accountability Office to audit member compliance within two years [S2] [S3].
Gives members 180 days after enactment (or after taking office) to complete divestment, easing the transition for members with existing portfolios [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to sell individual stocks and similar investments, move them into blind trusts, or switch to broad funds. Members whose wealth is tied to specific companies would bear the largest change, and members of both parties would lose the option of trading individual securities during their term.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Enforcement rests on the members' own annual certifications and on civil fines assessed by the House and Senate ethics committees, and a member can appeal a fine to a floor vote of their own chamber, so the bill leans on peer enforcement rather than an outside regulator [S3].
The 180-day window to sell, the ability to claim good-faith extensions, and the broad blind-trust carve-out give members significant room to delay or avoid divestment [S3].

Requiring divestment could steer members' wealth into blind trusts managed by financial professionals, and would be a real burden for members and spouses whose finances are concentrated in one company's stock, such as a family business holding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule is strong: a flat ban on trading and holding individual securities goes further than current disclosure-only law and directly removes the clearest conflict of interest in legislation. The weakness is enforcement, which relies on member self-certification, ethics committees made of members, and fines appealable to the full chamber. The bill would be more credible with an independent enforcer, but the burden it places on members is modest and they retain diversified investing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration and Ways and Means committees, neither ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Vicky Hartzler introduced the bill on January 25, 2022 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Committee on House Administration and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was scheduled, and the record shows no further action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, who kept the ability to hold and trade individual stocks while in office, are better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who kept trading rights

against.name: House committee leadership (House Administration; Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the two committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; neither committee reported it, so it never reached the floor

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support came from three House Republicans (the sponsor and two cosponsors); no Democrat signed on and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.note: Members and their spouses would lose the ability to hold or trade individual stocks, futures, and commodities while in office, and would face disgorgement and fines for violations. Their financial interest in keeping that ability runs against the public's interest in lawmakers without personal stakes in the laws they write.

Members would shift toward diversified funds, ETFs, and blind trusts, which could modestly change how congressional wealth is invested. The firms lose no significant revenue, and markets gain a small credibility benefit from removing possible congressional trading on inside knowledge.
